Markdown Content:
For requests with large payloads, you can reduce the size of the request body sent to the Cerebras API by using **msgpack encoding**, **gzip compression**, or both. This can meaningfully improve time-to-first-token (TTFT) for requests with long prompts.

## Encoding Options

The Cerebras API accepts the following request body encodings. The table shows the expected payload size reduction for each option:

| Content-Type | Description | Chat Completions 1 | Completions 2 |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `application/json` | Default JSON encoding | Baseline | Baseline |
| `application/vnd.msgpack` | msgpack binary encoding | up to ~5% | up to ~56% |
| `application/json` + `Content-Encoding: gzip` | JSON with gzip compression | up to ~98% | up to ~68% |
| `application/vnd.msgpack` + `Content-Encoding: gzip` | msgpack + gzip | up to ~98% | up to ~69% |

1 Measured against a 50k-token chat completions payload (206 KB JSON baseline).

2 Measured against a 50k token-ID completions payload (331 KB JSON baseline).You can use msgpack encoding or gzip compression independently, or combine them for maximum compression.Smaller request payloads reduce network transfer time, a contributing factor to TTFT. Actual TTFT improvement will vary, as network transfer is one of several factors that contribute to overall latency.

## When to Use Payload Optimization

Optimizing payload size with request compression is most beneficial for:

*   **Long prompts** – requests with long system prompts, extensive conversation history, or large code blocks. Gzip compression is the most effective option for these payloads.
*   **Token-ID completions** – `/v1/completions` payloads using integer token arrays benefit from both msgpack encoding and gzip compression
*   **Tool call-heavy payloads** – requests with many tool definitions or deeply nested JSON structures. Both msgpack encoding and gzip compression provide savings.

For small requests (under a few KB), the overhead of compression may outweigh the savings. Standard JSON encoding is fine for typical chat interactions.

## msgpack Encoding

msgpack is a binary serialization format that produces smaller payloads than equivalent JSON. To use it, serialize your request body with msgpack and set the `Content-Type` header to `application/vnd.msgpack`.

## Gzip Compression

You can gzip-compress any request body and set the `Content-Encoding: gzip` header. This works with both JSON and msgpack payloads.

## Combining Both

For maximum compression, use msgpack encoding with gzip compression:

Below is a single, comprehensive prompt that rewrites the provided technical description into a clear, implementation-focused instruction set for building the full feature from scratch. It preserves the source’s meaning about request-body optimization, supported encodings, expected benefits, and usage guidance, including the documented content types, compression combinations, and TTFT rationale.[1]

## Prompt

Build a complete, production-ready implementation of an API request payload optimization feature for an inference client and its supporting documentation, examples, and validation logic. The system must support four request body transmission modes for large API payloads: plain JSON, msgpack binary encoding, JSON compressed with gzip, and msgpack compressed with gzip. The implementation must treat payload-size reduction as a latency optimization mechanism for large requests, especially because smaller request bodies reduce network transfer time, which is one contributing factor to time-to-first-token. The system must also clearly communicate that actual end-to-end latency improvement will vary because network transfer time is only one of several contributors to total latency.[1]

Start by defining the feature scope and constraints. The implementation must support request optimization for large prompts, long system instructions, extensive conversation history, large code blocks, tool-call-heavy payloads with many tool definitions or deeply nested structures, and token-array completions payloads that use integer token IDs. The implementation must also explicitly avoid forcing compression for very small payloads, because the compression overhead may exceed the benefit for requests under a few kilobytes. Standard JSON must remain available as the default path for ordinary chat usage.[1]

Define the supported wire formats exactly. Support `application/json` as the default uncompressed baseline. Support `application/vnd.msgpack` as a binary request encoding alternative. Support gzip compression via the `Content-Encoding: gzip` header for both JSON and msgpack request bodies. Support the combined mode of msgpack plus gzip, using `Content-Type: application/vnd.msgpack` together with `Content-Encoding: gzip`, as the maximum-compression path. The system must be able to use msgpack independently, gzip independently, or both together.[1]

Implement serialization and transport as a deterministic pipeline. Accept a normalized in-memory request object. If the selected encoding mode is JSON, serialize the object to JSON bytes. If the selected encoding mode is msgpack, serialize the object to msgpack bytes. If gzip is enabled, compress the already-serialized byte stream using gzip without altering the semantic content of the request. Set headers strictly according to the chosen mode. Do not guess or omit headers. Ensure the HTTP client sends the exact serialized bytes produced by the pipeline and does not apply a second, conflicting transformation.[1]

Implement a mode-selection policy. The policy must allow manual forcing of any of the four supported modes, and it must also support an automatic mode that selects the most appropriate encoding based on request characteristics. In automatic mode, prefer gzip for long prompts and large textual payloads, because it is the most effective option for those payloads. Prefer msgpack plus gzip for maximum compression when the payload is large and the client environment supports msgpack cleanly. Prefer msgpack or msgpack plus gzip for token-ID completions payloads using integer arrays, because both msgpack encoding and gzip compression provide savings there. Prefer either msgpack, gzip, or both for tool-call-heavy and deeply nested request bodies. Fall back to standard JSON for small requests.[1]

Document the expected payload reduction figures exactly as reference guidance, not as hard guarantees. State that msgpack can reduce a chat completions payload by up to about 5 percent and a token-ID completions payload by up to about 56 percent. State that JSON plus gzip can reduce a chat completions payload by up to about 98 percent and a token-ID completions payload by up to about 68 percent. State that msgpack plus gzip can reduce a chat completions payload by up to about 98 percent and a token-ID completions payload by up to about 69 percent. Also document that the cited chat measurement was against a 50k-token chat completions payload with a 206 KB JSON baseline, and that the cited token-ID completions measurement was against a 50k token-ID completions payload with a 331 KB JSON baseline. Present these numbers as measured examples, not universal results.[1]

Implement robust API ergonomics. Expose a configuration surface that includes the selected payload mode, an automatic optimization option, optional size thresholds, and visibility into which transport mode was used for a given request. Include clear validation errors for unsupported combinations, malformed payloads, serialization failures, and compression failures. Ensure the implementation works with both chat-style request bodies and completions-style request bodies.[1]

Implement observability and verification. For each request, record the original serialized size, the final transmitted size, the selected content type, whether gzip was applied, and the percentage reduction achieved relative to the JSON baseline for that same request object when such comparison is available. Include automated tests that verify header correctness, byte-for-byte reproducibility, successful server interoperability for each mode, and correct fallback behavior for small payloads. Add benchmark coverage for large prompts, integer token arrays, and nested tool definitions.[1]

Produce full, unabridged, production-ready code and artifacts. Include the complete source files for the client implementation, serializer layer, compression layer, configuration layer, benchmark suite, tests, and end-user documentation. Include concrete examples demonstrating each of the four transmission modes and a maximum-compression example using msgpack with gzip. Do not include placeholders, stubs, mocks, pseudo-code, or simulated implementations. Every file must be complete and executable as delivered.[1]
